arXiv_CondMat.title: LatticeMind: A Validation-Gated Agentic Framework for Density Functional Theory Workflows
arXiv_CondMat.summary: First-principles calculations are rarely single solver calls: they are multistage workflows in which structures, settings, and saved densities must pass correctly between dependent stages. Language models can write a valid single input, but reliability collapses once stages are chained: a dropped dependency, wrong file handoff, or hallucinated keyword can invalidate results even when the solver runs, and such errors surface only after costly execution. We introduce LatticeMind, a validation-gated agentic framework that converts natural-language requests into executable, checkable density functional theory (DFT) projects. A workflow contract specifies required stages, files, and dependencies; deterministic validators inspect the project before any solver launch; failed checks trigger bounded repair; and reports remain traceable to project files. On a 44-case RESCU benchmark spanning total-energy, density-of-states, band-structure, magnetic, phonon workflows, three non-flagship LLM backends reproduced every reference value; 119 of 132 runs passed on the first validated plan and the rest after one repair cycle. Ablations identify the workflow contract and pre-execution validation as the principal reliability mechanisms; a conventional trial-and-repair baseline reaches 71% at twice the token cost per success. The same architecture reproduces every reference value on a 19-case VASP benchmark, demonstrating transfer across solvers. Beyond these task families, LatticeMind generated and validated the 23 inputs of a multistage study of Rh-induced electronic responses at a Rh$_6$/In$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$N photocatalyst interface. These results establish workflow contracts, deterministic validation, bounded repair, and traceable records as a practical foundation for reliable AI-assisted scientific computing, where preventable errors are caught before execution and the solver is never the first validator.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Vortex matter as a magnetically programmable metasurface for tuning near-field radiative heat transfer
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Near-field radiative heat transfer (NFRHT) is of great interest for energy conversion and thermal management. Recent work on NFRHT has shown that metasurfaces can enhance NFRHT and reshape its spectral characteristics. Here, we show that the vortex lattice of a type-II superconductor represents a self-assembled metasurface whose lattice dimensions, in contrast to most other metasurfaces, can be tuned by magnetic fields, allowing NFRHT to be varied by orders of magnitude. Specifically, we show that for two Nb surfaces at 4.2 K and separated by a 100 nm gap, NFRHT can be magnetically tuned by a factor >200. Further, we show that the tuning range grows upon cooling, exceeding 10^5 at 2 K, which is far beyond the order-unity modulation of many proposed schemes for tuning NFRHT. Our results establish vortex matter as a magnetically programmable thermal metasurface and open new opportunities for tuning the flow of heat at the nanoscale.

arXiv_CondMat.title: High-Field and Light-Dependent Magnetization Provides Evidence for Coexisting Granular Superconductivity and Superparamagnetism in Nitrogen-Doped Diamond
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We investigated the field-, temperature-, and time-dependent magnetic moment of a nitrogen-doped type Ib diamond in darkness and under monochromatic light with a low laser intensity of about 160 $\mu$W cm$^{-2}$. In darkness, below approximately 25 K, the magnetic moment exhibits unconventional hysteresis loops that can be explained by the coexistence of superparamagnetism and superconductivity in certain regions of the sample. Under illumination, this hysteresis largely disappears, leaving mainly the superparamagnetic contribution. Temperature-dependent measurements reveal an irreversibility below 25 K in darkness, which vanishes under illumination. Similarly, at 0.5 T and below 25 K, the time-dependent magnetization shows flux-creep-like behavior that disappears when the sample is illuminated. All light-induced changes are fully reversible: the magnetic properties measured in darkness are restored after the sample is heated above roughly 50 K. Removing the superparamagnetic contribution from magnetization measurements up to $\pm 14$ T reveals clear characteristics of a granular superconductor, namely, a well-defined penetration field $H_p \approx 2.6$ T and a critical field $H_{c2} \approx 10.6$ T. Based on theoretical considerations, we attribute the observed phenomena to the combined effects of internal stress and local variations in nitrogen concentration within localized regions that can be regarded as grains. This interpretation is supported by Raman and birefringence spectroscopy measurements on the same sample.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Zeeman Quantum Geometry of the Layer Pseudo-spin
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Two-dimensional layers coupled by position-dependent interlayer tunnelling host a layer pseudo-spin whose polarization is a controllable internal degree of freedom. We introduce the quantum geometry of this layer pseudo-spin: a mixed tensor formed from the interband Berry connection and the layer matrix element, which governs the response to an oscillating in-plane electric field. Because the layer pseudo-spin is an Ising-type scalar invariant under threefold rotation, its selection rules differ from those of a pseudovector spin. In a minimal two-band model, the layer-pseudo-spin quantum metric and Zeeman--Berry curvature are nonzero, while their zone integrals vanish. An in-plane drive therefore leaves the spatially averaged polarization unchanged at linear order but imprints a moir\'{e}-periodic intracell pattern, directly imageable by layer-resolved tunnelling. For twisted MoTe$_2$ bilayer, we quantify the local dipole modulation and identify the rectified, helicity-odd, and third-harmonic channels through which a net response appears at higher order.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Tailoring Dielectric Relaxation and Charge Transport in Amorphous Ge-Te-Se Phase-Change Materials through Yttrium Incorporation
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The Te(1-x)(GeSe0.5)Yx (x = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15) alloys were prepared by a melt-quenching method and characterized using dielectric spectroscopy. The dielectric parameters and electrical conductivity were evaluated to assess their potential for phase-change memory and other electronic applications. The temperature and frequency dependence of the dielectric constants, ac conductivity, and dielectric loss of prepared chalcogenide glassy alloys were investigated over the frequency range 1 Hz - 1 MHz, and the temperature range 302 - 422 K, below the glass transition temperature. Both dielectric loss and dielectric constant were found to decrease with increasing frequency and decreasing temperature. The observed dielectric loss change was interpreted using the Guintini model of dielectric dispersion, correlated barrier hopping (CBH) model, and orientation polarization. The Cole-Cole analysis confirmed a distribution of relaxation times and yielded activation energies consistent with the CBH conduction mechanism. The frequency dependence of the ac conductivity follows the power law (A{\omega}s), where the frequency exponent (s < 1) decreases with increasing temperature, further supporting the CBH conduction mechanism. The incorporation of Y increases the density of localized tail states, resulting in enhanced ac conductivity. These findings suggest that the investigated materials are promising candidates for future phase-change memory and other electronic device applications.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Achieving ultrahigh-temperature superfluidity in atomic Fermi gases by suppressing pairing fluctuations
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Achieving room-temperature superconductivity has been a long-sought goal of both the physics community and the industry. The superfluid transition temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$ of a Fermi system initially increases with increasing pairing strength between fermions following the mean-field prediction of the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory, and is then suppressed by pairing fluctuations as the strength increases further, which prevents $T_\mathrm{c}$ from becoming high. Here we propose a mechanism for suppressing pairing fluctuations using the synergy between population imbalance and momentum space confinement in lattice systems, enabling an ultrahigh $T_\mathrm{c}$ at moderately strong attraction. We show that in a three-dimensional optical lattice, strong Pauli exclusion between paired and excess majority fermions pushes up the pair excitation energy and suppresses finite-momentum pairing fluctuations. The mechanism is general to any lattice with a finite Brillouin zone; the optimal imbalance is modest ($p\lesssim 0.1$), keeping the Zeeman field small and avoiding orbital complications. The gapped pair dispersion at moderate imbalance exponentially suppresses thermal condensate depletion, providing a testable signature. The gapped dispersion, enhanced condensate fraction, and pseudogap reduction are all accessible in present-day experiments. This work opens new avenues toward room-temperature superconductivity.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Heat-current-induced nonreciprocal phonon damping
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Time-reversal symmetry enforces equal equilibrium linewidths for time-reversed phonon modes at opposite wave vectors. Here we show that a steady heat current can produce nonreciprocal anharmonic damping even in centrosymmetric nonmagnetic crystals. The effect arises from nonequilibrium occupations of scattering partners, which change the statistical weights of time-reversed three-phonon channels while their squared matrix elements remain equal. Within the single-mode relaxation-time approximation, we derive a linewidth correction that is linear in the temperature gradient and odd under wave-vector reversal. The response depends on scattering-partner velocities and equilibrium lifetimes and retains signed channel weights absent from the equilibrium linewidth. First-principles calculations for centrosymmetric MgO and diamond yield nonzero, mode-dependent linewidth corrections at selected finite wave vectors, demonstrating the mechanism in both ionic and covalent crystals. Reversing the heat current at fixed local temperature exchanges the broadening and narrowing of paired modes. This current-reversible linewidth contrast provides a spectral signature of occupation feedback, with potential implications for nonlinear phonon transport.

arXiv_CondMat.title: MOFFieldBench: A Machine Learning Benchmark for Continuous Electronic Fields in Metal-Organic Frameworks
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Machine-learning models for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) predominantly rely on atomic structures, whereas electron-density (ED) and electrostatic-potential (ESP) fields remain underexplored as scalable learning representations. These continuous fields encode complementary spatial and electronic information relevant to structure-property relationships, particularly pore geometry and guest-framework interactions, but costly first-principles calculations, storage requirements and the scarcity of systematically aligned datasets limit their broader use. Here we introduce MOFFieldBench, a multimodal benchmark comprising approximately 46,000 MOFs with one-to-one aligned crystallographic structures, ED fields and ESP fields. A unified workflow integrates field generation, error-controlled compression and sparse point-cloud representation, supporting field reconstruction, prediction of 13 material properties, multimodal property prediction and pairwise cross-modal retrieval. ED and ESP provide competitive representations for pore geometry, adsorption and separation properties. Multimodal fusion improves several prediction tasks relative to the best unimodal reference, supporting complementary predictive roles for atomic structures and electronic fields. Learned ED reconstruction closely approximates first-principles reference densities, while predicted-density initialization reduces self-consistent-field calculation time by 13.59\% on average in paired tests. These results support electronic fields as practical, informative learning modalities and establish MOFFieldBench as a resource for studying representation choice, multimodal learning and electronic-field-driven MOF modelling.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Field Theory of the Gutzwiller Projection
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The Gutzwiller projection produces a well-known ansatz for spin-liquid and quantum Hall ground-state wavefunctions that is amenable to numerical simulation, with the Laughlin wavefunction being the most celebrated example. A long-standing issue is the precise relation between the Gutzwiller projection and the closely related parton gauge theory. Here, we clarify this issue by providing a field-theoretic description of the Gutzwiller projection. In a path integral description, the universal physics of the projected state is described in terms of a gauge field supported on a temporal slab of vanishing width $\epsilon \rightarrow 0$ coupled to the bulk matter fields. We analytically derive the universal physics of various Gutzwiller projected states. Our construction is also applicable to discrete symmetries, and we use it to analyze various projected SPT states. Among our results, we show that the Gutzwiller projection is not a good ansatz for the long-distance properties of $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquids, spinon Fermi surface spin liquids or composite Fermi liquids, and that the Gutzwiller projection of a quantum spin Hall state has only quasi-long range order. In contrast, in examples where the gauge field is gapped, including Laughlin states, $\mathbb{Z}_2$ spin liquids and Luttinger liquids, we show that the slab gauge theory from Gutzwiller projection reproduces the correct universal physics of the full parton gauge theory. We also present a generalization of our field theory that describes $G$-intertwining defects, with application to self-duality defects of recent theoretical interest.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Spectral signatures of hidden order and hidden quantum critical points
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Hidden-order phases elude the conventional Ginzburg-Landau framework: although they spontaneously break symmetry, their order remains invisible to standard local two-point correlators. Instead, they are typically characterized by nonlocal (string) order parameters and are believed to underlie a range of exotic quantum states, such as symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases. While hidden correlations have previously been detected through nonlocal observables in quantum gas microscope experiments, in realistic solid-state systems multipoint observables are typically inaccessible and the signatures of hidden order remain largely unexplored. In this work, we show that hidden order in doped spin chains can be directly probed through dynamical two-point response functions measurable by resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) and neutron scattering. Focusing on a minimal model, we numerically identify clear spectral fingerprints of both the hidden-order phase, its associated hidden quantum critical point as well as a specific group of gapless SPT phases. Complementing our numerical results with analytical insights, we uncover the microscopic origin of these spectral signatures and demonstrate how they emerge from the interplay between spin and charge degrees of freedom. Together, our results establish spectroscopy as a practical probe of hidden order and gapless SPT phases and provide a unified understanding of the low-energy physics governing these unconventional quantum phases.

arXiv_CondMat.title: An efficient approach to electron-phonon coupling calculations of heterostructures within an all-electron framework
arXiv_CondMat.summary: A major challenge in calculating electron-phonon coupling at interfaces from first principles is the prohibitive computational cost due to the large supercells involved. Here, we present an efficient approach, which builds the electron-phonon matrix of weakly bound heterostructures from the properties of the isolated layers. The two key ingredients, the dynamical matrices and the potential response, are constructed in two steps. In the expansion step, these quantities are folded from the unit cells onto the supercell through an exact Fourier mapping. In the addition step, the interatomic force constants and the potential responses of the heterostructure are assembled blockwise from the corresponding quantities of the isolated layers, neglecting the weak interlayer contribution. The method is implemented in the electron-phonon module of the all-electron full-potential code exciting, enabling efficient calculations of the electron-phonon self-energy. We demonstrate the approach for the phonon dispersion and spectral functions of bilayer WSe$_2$ and pyridine/MoS$_2$, in comparison with exact reference calculations.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Quantum Oscillations across Hole Crystallization in Rhombohedral Graphene
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Recent quantum-oscillation measurements in rhombohedral graphene reveal an abrupt increase in the dominant frequency and the emergence of additional frequencies as the carrier density is lowered toward superconductivity. Noninteracting band models can account for multiple frequencies but do not explain the upward jump. We show that these features can arise from two competing fates of the inner hole pocket in an annular Fermi sea: collapse into a simply connected Fermi liquid or crystallization into an anticrystal, in which localized holes coexist with itinerant electrons. Pocket collapse contracts the outer Fermi contour at fixed density, whereas hole crystallization preserves a larger contour that supports magnetic-breakdown orbits. This contrast provides a possible explanation for the frequency jump, while additional reconstructed orbits produce a multitone spectrum. Our results support the anticrystal as a candidate normal state near superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Exact spectral integrability of a finite-channel random Schr\"odinger operator: from fermionization of the Dyson--Riccati gas to Kontsevich integral
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We solve exactly, for arbitrary finite channel number $N$, the Riccati dynamics of a quasi-one-dimensional random matrix Schr\"odinger operator with Hermitian white-noise potential in the $\beta=2$ unitary symmetry class. The associated Dyson--Riccati eigenvalue gas admits an exact free-fermion representation at any sample length $L$, which in the limit $L\to \infty$ expresses the density of states and the total Lyapunov growth rate exactly through a single Airy Hankel $\tau$-function providing multichannel generalization of $N=1$ Halperin--Thouless formulas. The $\tau-$function further admits an outgoing-contour Kontsevich matrix Airy integral representation. Its saddle-point and double-scaling analyses give, in a unified way, the finite-channel density Lifshitz tail, and the large-$N$ spectral edge. In particular, for $N\gg 1$ the sharp $N=\infty$ edge is softened within an $N^{-4/5}$ spectral window, with its profile governed by the tritronqu\'ee solution of Painlev\'e I. We conjecture universality of this quasi-one-dimensional scaling edge profile for a broad class of $\beta=2$ random band matrices.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Ballistic transport and crystallographic control in altermagnetic quantum rings
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We study coherent two-terminal transport through a finite-width $d$-wave altermagnetic quantum ring with nonmagnetic leads. A confined Aharonov--Bohm flux remains exactly $h/e$ periodic and, in the symmetric one-mode geometry, produces an exact half-flux transmission zero. A perpendicular field shifts the interference pattern according to an effective area $A_{\rm eff}=1.0342\,\pi r_0^2$ and the altermagnetic splitting resolves the common zero into nearby spin-dependent nodes. Rotating the crystal reverses the transmitted spin, whereas the mirror orientation $\theta_A=\pi/4$ is exactly spin degenerate. For a $50$~nm reference ring, sub-tesla fields yield windows with $|P_T|>0.99$, the most accessible of which requires a uniform field alone and no confined flux. Finite-bias, thermal, disorder, Zeeman, and spin-conserving voltage-probe calculations show that the polarization is appreciably more stable than individual coherent-resonance amplitudes. These results identify interference-node positions, flux periodicity, and crystal-controlled spin polarization as experimentally useful signatures of an altermagnetic mesoscopic interferometer.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Diffusive Description of Superconducting Single-Photon Detectors Using Quantum Mechanics
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The methodology of non-Hermitian quantum mechanics is employed to parameterize the dynamics of coupled classical diffusion equations describing low- and high-energy quasiparticles in superconducting single-photon detectors in one to three spatial dimensions.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Density Accelerated Relaxation in Active Passive Colloidal Networks with Competing Interactions
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We investigate quasi-2D active-passive colloidal mixtures with electric field-mediated non-identical interactions: unlike species attract and like species repel. Mapping the steady states across total area fraction and active particle area fraction identifies the regime of active percolated network formation among active fluid and clustered states. Within the percolated network regime, relaxation speeds up with increasing density, contrary to expectations for dense particulate gels. Particle-resolved dynamics and microstructure link this acceleration to activity-driven rearrangements enabled by asymmetric interactions.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Nanoscale chemical engineering of Ti3C2Tx MXene multilayers through in situ electron beam irradiation in a TEM
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Defect engineering in low-dimensional materials is a powerful approach to tailor their structure and chemistry at the atomic scale, with high relevance for tuning physical properties. Here, we apply this strategy to MXenes, one of the largest families of two-dimensional (2D) materials, and demonstrate the use of a highly focused scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) beam for the structural and chemical nanoengineering of titanium carbide (Ti3C2Tx) multilayers. By adjusting the beam energy, electron dose, and scanning parameters, Ti3C2Tx multilayers were irradiated at 80 and 300 keV and characterized in situ using annular dark-field imaging and electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS). The irradiation induces gradual structural and chemical modifications, largely driven by the selective sputtering of atomic species and MXene layers. We identify irradiation conditions that selectively remove Cl or F surface terminations while largely preserving the Ti3C2 framework, whereas other conditions promote preferential carbon removal, in agreement with theoretical predictions. Most notably, electron irradiation drives the migration and accumulation of initially dilute nitrogen impurities within the irradiated regions, leading to the formation of nitrogen-rich titanium carbonitride (Ti3CyNzTx) nanodomains embedded in the Ti3C2Tx multilayers. These laterally patterned carbide/carbonitride architectures constitute in-plane MXene heterostructures with nanometer-scale spatial control. These results demonstrate that electron irradiation can be used to locally tailor MXene composition and create nanoscale architectures beyond those accessible through conventional chemical synthesis.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Soft elasticity of soft shells
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Soft modes of a shell are one-parameter families of non-trivial deformations that preserve the elastic energy. We identify all soft modes of the soft shells described by the variational theory of put forward by Sonnet and Virga (2025). They are seen to be strictly connected with the Bonnet families, a special class of solutions to the problem posited by Bonnet, who asked whether there exist non-trivial isometries that preserve the mean curvature. Differential geometry deems as equivalent all surfaces in one and the same Bonnet family, but continuum mechanics is interested more specifically in soft deformation modes and the shapes they traverse, as they may describe ways to ignite fluctuations of soft shells that ideally require no energy to be activated. We give a general criterion for the existence of soft modes and a method to construct them based on a cascade of path integrations. We apply both criterion and method to some exemplary cases.
authors: Andre M. Sonnet, Epifanio G. Virga

arXiv_CondMat.title: Structure and Dynamics of Defects in Two-Dimensional Nematic Liquid Crystals
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Topological defects in nematic liquid crystals have recently received renewed interest due to their important role in non-equilibrium active materials and developing biological systems. While many studies have focused on simulating defect behaviors in these non-equilibrium situations, there has also been recent progress in our analytical understanding of defect morphology and behavior in a number of complicated regimes, such as intricate boundary conditions, anisotropic elasticity, or the presence of flows. Here, we review the analytical theory of disclination structure and dynamics in two-dimensional nematic liquid crystals, highlighting recent methods and results.
authors: Cody D. Schimming, Daniel A. Beller

arXiv_CondMat.title: Intrinsic Curvature Controls Spontaneous Entanglement of Elastic Rods
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We report results from an experimental investigation on the role of intrinsic curvature in the spontaneous entanglement of elastic rods subjected to controlled tumbling. We examine two distinct entanglement mechanisms, knotting and locking, in a statistical ensemble of straight and helical rods with varying arc length and natural curvature. Our primary finding is that natural curvature exerts a dominant, non-monotonic influence on knotting, with a critical curvature that suppresses knot formation and significantly reduces the probability of knotting relative to equivalent straight rods. In contrast, locking is largely insensitive to curvature and scales primarily with rod length. These results, obtained for the macroscopic experimental system studied here, identify geometric parameters that govern distinct entanglement modes in tumbled elastic rods and may inform entanglement processes in microscopic filamentary systems such as DNA.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Reaction-induced Localized Annealing for On-chip Materials Discovery
arXiv_CondMat.summary: On-chip thermal processing is a key technology for materials discovery across all disciplines of the natural sciences. Here, we present a microfabricated heat-delivery platform that enables reaction-induced localized on-chip annealing up to 1400{\deg}C. A buried reactive multilayer combined with a nanometric diffusion barrier provide ultra-fast heating and quenching rates on the order of 10$^6${\deg}C s$^{-1}$ as illustrated by the generation of ultra-high aspect ratio microstructures during rapid-solidification and the stabilization of dopant-free tetragonal zirconia at room temperature. Rapid kinetics also enable the observation of transient states of capillary-driven hole collapse in melts. Our work expands localized high-temperature processing routes and offers a material-independent approach for rapid screening of multidimensional nanomaterials on and off-equilibrium.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Fully Automated Wannier Disentanglement via Projectability Selection in Gaussian and Augmented Plane-Wave Frameworks
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Constructing the frozen manifold for entangled bands requires balancing exact reproduction of the target bands with sufficient variational freedom to build a well-localized subspace from the broader Bloch pool. We present a workflow that systematically determines the energy ceiling for a target number of selected Wannier projections, freezing every Bloch state below this threshold across the sampled k-mesh. By measuring projectability, the spectral weight of each Bloch state projected onto the target localized basis, the workflow detects missing conduction channels and quantifies discrepancies between orbital character and energy-based freezing. In comparisons where we controlled the extent of the energy ceiling, freezing all sub-ceiling states is generally favored over projectability-based frozen states. Of the seven materials we tested, freezing all sub-ceiling states lowers the band error on four from between 11 meV and 1.2 eV to 18 meV or less, and matches the projectability-based choice to within about 2 meV on the remaining three. In each of the four, projectability-based frozen states give the lower spread, showing that spread alone cannot identify the better model. With the frozen states held fixed, the workflow minimizes the gauge-invariant spread, constructs the gauge from density-matrix columns on atomic orbitals, and passes an isolated set of bands to Wannier90 for localization. The workflow is implemented in two programs for seamless high-throughput Wannierization with WIEN2k (wien2wannier) and CRYSTAL (LCAO2Wannier). Using a single set of calibrated defaults, the CRYSTAL implementation with analytic overlaps produces models that reproduce the reference bands of five cells, from bulk h-BN in a joint valence-and-conduction model to a magnetic framework with 1424 orbitals. The WIEN2k implementation produces eight such models from seven calculations.
authors: William P. Comaskey, Jose L. Mendoza-Cortes

arXiv_CondMat.title: Learning the Geometry of Materials Space with Trained Neural Tangent Kernels
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Neural networks trained to predict materials properties learn representations whose physical content can be difficult to extract. We use the neural tangent kernel (NTK), evaluated at trained parameters, to recover the geometry learned by a network that predicts superconducting transition temperatures from elemental composition alone. Kernel ridge regression with the trained NTK closely reproduces the network's predictive performance and substantially outperforms regression with the initial kernel. Spectral analysis and multidimensional scaling reveal a geometry dominated by a small number of directions. Clustering and local neighborhood analysis organize compounds into recognizable superconducting families and connect materials with related chemical and correlated-electron properties despite substantial differences in $T_c$. These results establish trained tangent kernels as practical probes of learned materials representations, connecting property prediction with the exploration of materials space.

arXiv_CondMat.title: In Situ Thermal Preparation by CO$_2$-Laser and Chemical Characterization of Oxide Substrates Across Multiple Crystallographic Orientations
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Atomically flat and chemically controlled oxide substrate surfaces are essential for high-quality epitaxial growth of complex materials and heterostructures. Previous studies have demonstrated in situ thermal preparation of selected oxide substrates, primarily focusing on conventional low-index orientations such as SrTiO$_3$ (100) and LaAlO$_3$ (100). Here, we extend these methodologies to a broader range of oxide substrates and crystallographic orientations, including challenging polar surfaces. We present a systematic study of the in situ thermal preparation of SrTiO$_3$ (100), SrTiO$_3$ (111), GdScO$_3$ (110), LaAlO$_3$ (111), (LaAlO$_3$)$_{0.3}$(Sr$_2$AlTaO$_6$)$_{0.7}$ (001), and NdGaO$_3$ (110) single crystal substrates. The substrates are annealed in a vacuum chamber under a controlled oxygen background environment using a CO$_2$ laser heating system. The optimized annealing conditions produce atomically flat step-and-terrace structures, long-range surface crystallinity, and effectively clean surfaces across all the investigated substrates. Our results establish a versatile, reproducible, and broadly applicable platform for the in situ preparation of oxide substrates immediately prior to epitaxial growth. These results also provide practical guidelines for interface engineering and surface-sensitive investigations of complex materials.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Chiral magnetic excitations in the RMn6Sn6 kagome metals (R=Tb, Ho, Er, and Y)
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Recent inelastic neutron scattering (INS) investigations of the kagome metal TbMn6Sn6 reveal novel chiral magnetic excitations associated with the kagome layer. These excitations appear to have an itinerant character with a large energy scale (> 100 meV) and heavy damping; however, the origin of these excitations, which are not predicted by local moment linear spin-wave theory, is not understood. Here, we use INS to show that chiral excitations are also found in RMn6Sn6 compounds with R=Tb, Ho, Er, and Y having uniaxial, tilted, planar ferrimagnet, and planar double-spiral magnetic structures, respectively. Thus, the chiral excitations exist regardless of the magnetic structure. Additionally, R=Er and Y demonstrate that the chiral mode intensity is weaker in planar magnetic structures, suggesting that excitations are transverse to the local Mn moment direction. The chiral excitations appear only at L=odd positions in the Brilloun zone, and correspond to chiral spin exciations of the same handedness within each kagome layer, and pi out-of-phase between layers.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Steering of topological criticality in the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain via non-Hermitian substitutional impurities
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We investigate the topological phase in a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain in the presence of a finite concentration of non-Hermitian substitutional impurities. Our primary focus is the discovery of a deterministic mechanism to actively reconfigure the topological phase boundaries by introducing site-dependent, non-reciprocal intracell and intercell hopping amplitudes. Specifically, breaking the internal structural symmetry of the non-reciprocal impurity hoppings induces a targeted macroscopic displacement of the critical point. This mechanism allows for the controlled expansion or compression of the topological phase strictly via local defect asymmetry. We validate this boundary displacement through finite-size scaling analysis. The extracted correlation length critical exponents ($\nu \approx 1.455$ and $\nu \approx 1.397$ for symmetric and asymmetric configurations, respectively) confirm a disorder-induced departure from the pristine SSH universality class, with the exponent diverging at high defect densities. We also report an impurity-induced real-to-complex spectral transition geometrically characterized by the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect. Ultimately, our results establish how isolated non-Hermitian asymmetries cooperatively interact to deterministically shift macroscopic topological protection.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Nanocrystalline cubic boron arsenide growth on GaAs(100) by gas source molecular beam epitaxy
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Cubic boron arsenide (c-BAs) is a promising ultrahigh thermal conductivity semiconductor, but its direct synthesis on lattice-mismatched substrates remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate the synthesis of nanocrystalline c-BAs thin films on GaAs(100) substrates using gas source molecular beam epitaxy. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals an optimal growth temperature window of 250-400 C to maintain near stoichiometry and suppress severe arsenic loss. Surface and structural characterizations via atomic force microscopy, reflection high-energy electron diffraction, and grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction demonstrate a Volmer-Weber 3D island growth mode and a preferential crystallographic alignment with the GaAs substrate. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy confirms a chemically sharp interface without gallium interdiffusion into the c-BAs layer. These findings establish an initial step for the integration of c-BAs into advanced thermal and optoelectronic platforms.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Magnetic-Field-Induced Darkening of Bright Excitons in a MoWSe$_2$ Monolayer Alloy
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Magnetic fields are widely used to brighten spin-forbidden dark excitons, but the inverse effect on an optically bright exciton has remained largely unexplored. We demonstrate the complementary phenomenon of magnetic-field-induced darkening of a bright exciton in Mo$_{0.68}$W$_{0.32}$Se$_2$. At 4.2 K, an in-plane magnetic field up to 25 T activates a dark-exciton line 14.2$\pm$1.3 meV below the bright exciton while suppressing the bright-exciton emission by about 85\%. A bright-dark mixing model quantitatively captures the coupled energy and intensity evolution with an effective in-plane $g$ factor of $|g_{\parallel}|=5.2\pm0.2$. Alloying is crucial to the effect, as it brings the system close to the bright-dark crossover, where a small bright-dark splitting is combined with unusually strong in-plane magnetic coupling. This places the system in a regime where field-induced level repulsion raises the bright-like branch and strongly depletes its thermal population. These results identify a general route to magnetic control of exciton populations through engineering of the bright-dark hierarchy.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Charge-conserving creation and annihilation of topological phase singularities in atomically thin semiconductors
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides provide a promising material platform for optical phase manipulation, as rapid variations in their dielectric functions can give rise to topological phase singularities (PSs). However, PS evolution while preserving topological charge conservation has not yet been investigated in exciton enabled PS systems. Here, using atomically thin MoS2 films on sapphire as a model system, we theoretically and experimentally demonstrate that the evolution of dielectric dispersion determines the creation, trajectory, merging, and annihilation of optical PSs under topological charge conservation. By varying the MoS2 film thickness, we experimentally realize this evolution through the gradual shrinking of the high energy n-k dispersion loop, which modifies its intersection with the zero reflection condition. Our results provide a general strategy for exploring and manipulating topological optical states.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Rashba-controlled emergence and reversal of critical-field anisotropy in p-wave magnet--superconductor hybrids
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We show that tuning Rashba spin-orbit coupling can change the in-plane field direction along which an $s$-wave superconductor is most susceptible to Zeeman depairing. We consider a two-dimensional $s$-wave superconductor subject to an odd-parity exchange field induced by a $p$-wave magnet. Without Rashba coupling, the out-of-plane exchange field enhances the in-plane critical field but leaves its angular response exactly isotropic, despite the anisotropic magnetic spin texture. Minimizing the Bogoliubov--de Gennes grand potential over uniform singlet pairing, we find that increasing Rashba coupling first generates and then reverses the principal-axis critical-field contrast, switching the minimum-critical-field direction by $90^{\circ}$. Equal principal-axis fields at the intervening compensation point coexist with residual angular modulation. We interpret the reversal through competing momentum-dependent depairing contributions from the magnetic and Rashba spin textures, while the on-site singlet pairing channel remains unchanged. Direction-dependent discontinuous collapses of the order parameter further shape the critical-field curves. These results identify a tunable directional paramagnetic response within the uniform-pairing sector. In heterostructures with sufficient electrostatic tunability of interfacial Rashba coupling, this reversal would enable gate control of the easy-depairing axis without reorienting the magnetic texture.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Magnetic-Field Effects on the Electronic States of the K$_4$ Lattice
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We investigate the electronic states of the K$_4$ lattice in a uniform magnetic field within a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. The K$_4$ lattice is a \rev{noncentrosymmetric three-dimensional network with triple-Dirac cones at the $\Gamma$ and H points}. By fixing the Bloch momentum component parallel to the field, the Peierls-substituted tight-binding problem reduces to an effective two-dimensional problem and yields a Hofstadter spectrum \rev{whose self-similar subpatterns reflect the geometry of the lattice projected onto the plane perpendicular to the field}. A square-like substructure emerges on the flux scale $\phi = 1/8$ for $\bm{B}\parallel[100]$, and honeycomb- and triangular-like substructures emerge on the finer scale $\phi = 1/32$ for $\bm{B}\parallel[111]$\rev{. Here $\phi$ is the flux through the elementary plaquette of the projected lattice, and these scales correspond to one flux quantum per projected unit cell. Owing to the screw axes of the chiral K$_4$ network, the field-parallel momentum acts as an additional flux, which, for commensurate values of this momentum, shifts the spectrum along the flux axis and brings the second triple-Dirac cone at the H point into the magnetic spectrum}. In the weak-field limit, we derive the Landau-level structure from a low-energy effective Hamiltonian around the $\Gamma$ point. The three-component nature of the triple-Dirac cone gives rise to a cubic secular equation, whose solutions describe how a pseudospin-flat branch coexists with two relativistic Landau ladders \rev{and a single chiral $n=0$ level dispersing linearly along the field, in agreement with the lattice calculation}.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Finite-temperature spectral functions of lattice polarons with process tensors
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We develop a process tensor approach for calculating the finite-temperature spectral functions of lattice polarons. We show that the finite-temperature phonon influence functional can be expressed as the elementwise exponential of a low-rank matrix product state, enabling an efficient summation of electron worldlines. An embedding construction embeds worldlines of different propagation times into a single matrix product state. This construction yields the propagator over the full simulated time interval in a single calculation. We benchmark this approach against available finite-temperature density-matrix renormalization group results for the one-dimensional Holstein polaron. We further obtain numerically converged spectra for the two-dimensional Holstein polaron. The spectra reveal a progressive transfer of spectral weight from coherent spectral features into an incoherent background with increasing temperature.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Orbital Magnetization within Self-Consistent Hartree-Fock via an Envelope Theorem
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Orbital magnetization is an elementary thermodynamic response function of a quantum system: the derivative of the grand potential with respect to magnetic field. However, naive perturbation theory is fraught with difficulties, as even infinitesimal magnetic fields shatter any bands into a Hofstadter butterfly spectrum. Even at the self-consistent Hartree-Fock (mean field) level, rigorous formulas for the orbital magnetization have only become available within the last year. This work provides a straightforward derivation of orbital magnetization at the mean field level using a completely real-space approach. The key tools used are the magnetic perturbation theory developed in the 1960s and an envelope theorem, which is a standard result in the calculus of variations. For simplicity, we restrict to insulating states at zero temperature on the infinite plane. We also discuss the natural connections to projected position operators and quantum geometry, as well as practical numerical computations.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Lattice symmetry breaking and strain control of single-$\mathbf{q}$ magnetism in Na$_3$Co$_2$SbO$_6$
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Distinguishing single-$\mathbf{q}$ from multi-$\mathbf{q}$ magnetism constrains microscopic spin Hamiltonians. Here we determine the ground state of the candidate Kitaev magnet Na$_3$Co$_2$SbO$_6$ through its coupling to the lattice. High-resolution neutron diffraction reveals a spontaneous monoclinic-to-triclinic distortion at the magnetic transition, in contrast to the absence of detectable lattice-symmetry breaking in triple-$\mathbf{q}$ Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$. Together with strain-selective magnetic responses, this identifies single-$\mathbf{q}$ order in Na$_3$Co$_2$SbO$_6$ over the proposed symmetry-preserving double-$\mathbf{q}$ state. Uniaxial compression along a low-symmetry in-plane direction achieves the domain selection that magnetic-field training could not, revealing the intrinsic field-induced phase boundaries of the dominant domain. These results establish strain as a symmetry-conjugate field for magnetic domains and highlight magnetoelastic coupling as a route to diagnose, manipulate, and potentially tune magnetic states.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Pressure-induced superconductivity in a bilayer metal
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We propose a model that explains the mechanism of pressure-induced superconductivity in a bilayer metal. Four types of pair potentials are assumed for a Cooper pair consisting of two electrons on different layers. Absence of local inversion symmetry gives rise to the spin-orbit coupling which is antisymmetric in the two layers. We assume that external pressure enhances the hybridization between the two layers. The stability of the superconducting states is well explained by the frequency symmetry of the induced pairing correlations by these potentials. Pressure-induced superconductivity emerges when the following two conditions are realized. (i) The spin-orbit coupling induces the odd-frequency pairing correlations and suppresses superconductivity at ambient pressure. (ii) The interplay between the spin-orbit coupling and the hybridization induces the additional pairing correlation that belongs to an even-frequency symmetry class. We briefly discuss the relevance of our model to real materials.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Symmetry Enriched Criticality from Kennedy Tasaki Self-Duality
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The interplay between topology and quantum criticality has established symmetry enriched criticality as a new paradigm beyond conventional frameworks in condensed matter and statistical physics. However, the conditions under which such criticality emerges remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that a broad class of symmetry enriched critical points separating symmetry protected topological (SPT) and spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) phases is governed by Kennedy Tasaki (KT) self duality. At these criticalities, the KT transformation that interchanges the SPT and SSB phases acts as a self-dual noninvertible symmetry, endowing the critical points with nontrivial topological characteristics. We numerically demonstrate this mechanism in $\mathbb{Z}_{n} \times \mathbb{Z}_{n}$ cluster qudit chains and further argue that it naturally extends to higher dimensions, providing a duality based criterion for identifying symmetry-enriched criticality across dimensions.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Andreev Scattering Driven Surface Photogalvanic Effect
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The surface photogalvanic effect is a powerful tool for generating macroscopic direct currents in centrosymmetric film structures via asymmetric scattering of carriers at film boundaries. Here, we uncover a fundamentally distinct regime of photoinduced transport in normal metal-superconductor heterostructures, in which the macroscopic photocurrent is governed by Andreev scattering at the interface rather than by classical scattering. We demonstrate that the interplay between asymmetric surface scattering and Andreev retroreflection yields a giant, strongly frequency-dependent anomalous photocurrent. Strikingly, the electron-hole conversion at the normal-superconducting interface dictates a macroscopic sign reversal of the photogalvanic current across the superconducting transition, and induces non-analytic spectral kinks exactly at the pairing gap frequency. Our results establish the Andreev reflection-driven surface photogalvanic effect as a platform for optical control of superconducting correlations and suggest a direct, non-invasive spectroscopic probe for gap dynamics in hybrid quantum devices.
authors: V. M. Kovalev, I. G. Savenko

arXiv_CondMat.title: A high-speed, large-aperture 3D printed laser shutter for cold atom experiments
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Cold atom experiments require optical shutters with rapid and repeatable actuation. Existing solutions often involve high cost, limited aperture diameter and slow transitioning. We present a 3D-printable shutter design featuring a large aperture of 4.5 mm diameter, low-cost assembly, and robust performance. The device achieves switching times of $399\pm8~\mu$s with delays of $2.7\pm0.2$ ms for a fully illuminated aperture, with four different shutters demonstrating repeatable performance. We measure the shutter speed to be $7.0\pm0.1$ m/s. This approach offers an accessible, scalable solution for cold atom and other optical experiments requiring multiple shutters with precise light control and avoids the need to resize or precision-align a beam through an aperture.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Non-uniform grids to accelerate electron-phonon coupling calculations for superconductivity
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Efficient and accurate evaluation of electron-phonon interactions is essential for predictive superconductivity calculations, but dense Brillouin zone sampling requirements pose a major computational bottleneck. To overcome this, we introduce an accelerated, highly scalable framework that combines a double delta truncation scheme with non-uniform Farey grids in both $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ space. The truncation strategy significantly reduces computational cost by restricting integration to states satisfying energy constraints near the Fermi level, while the Farey grids dynamically resolve sampling errors from localized scattering and stabilize convergence. Applied to elemental aluminium and several high-pressure hydrides, this combined methodology reduces computational cost by up to two orders of magnitude and yields electron-phonon coupling constants and superconducting critical temperatures Tc typically within about 5% of full-grid benchmarks. This approach overcomes sampling bottlenecks associated with dense uniform grids, making accurate, low-cost predictions of superconductivity in complex quantum materials feasible.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Superconducting weak links at substrate steps in bilayer nickelate films
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Ambient-pressure superconductivity above 40 K has been realized in bilayer nickelate thin films on SrLaAlO$_4$ (001), yet resistive measurements often exhibit incomplete zero-resistance states and/or two-step superconducting transitions of unresolved origin. We show that these features arise from superconducting weak links at substrate step-terrace structures. A direct correlation between the azimuthal-angle-dependent two-step transition and step-terrace orientation establishes this connection, further supported by atomic-scale visualization of structurally disrupted regions at step terraces. Modeling the films as pristine (weak-link) regions with higher (lower) transition temperature reproduces essential features of the two-step transition using both a simple model and finite-element simulations. Transport measurements further reveal a strong dependence of transition characteristics - and even the occurrence of superconductivity itself - on average terrace width. These results identify step-induced weak links as the microscopic origin of two-step transitions in bilayer nickelate films, providing a framework for understanding anisotropic and percolative transport, and a route to superconducting devices.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Good-$\Gamma$ Numbers: A Shell-Optimized Route to the Thermodynamic Limit in Quantum Monte Carlo Calculations of the High-Density Two-Dimensional Electron Gas
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Single-particle finite-size errors remain a central obstacle in quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations of periodic systems, conventionally reduced via twist averaging (TA). Here we introduce Good-$\Gamma$ (GG) particle numbers as system sizes $N$ at which the $\Gamma$-point Hartree--Fock (HF) energy of the high-density two-dimensional uniform electron gas (2D UEG) lies anomalously close to its thermodynamic-limit (TL) value. All results in this work concern the 2D UEG in its high-density Fermi-liquid regime, $r_s=1$--$4$. We systematically investigate the kinetic- and exchange-energy errors, $\Delta KE(N)$ and $\Delta EX(N)$, that underlie this one-body finite-size-error cancellation across four densities and both spin polarizations. We then compare diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) energies extrapolated to the TL from GG-$N$ sequences against twist-averaged extrapolations at the same densities and polarizations, finding agreement to within a fraction of a millihartree in every case, independent of whether a $1/N$ or an $N^{-5/4}$ extrapolation form is used.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Spin fluctuations and nearly isotropic quasiparticles in the doped three-dimensional Hubbard model
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Away from half filling and above its Neel temperature, the three-dimensional Hubbard model is a paramagnetic metal with antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations, where controlled momentum-resolved results have been lacking. Using connected-determinant diagrammatic Monte Carlo, we compute the momentum-resolved self-energy for n = 0.4-0.95, T/t = 0.05-0.33 and U/t = 4-8, and the full-zone spin susceptibility at twelve of these points, focusing on U/t = 4. At U/t = 4 and toward half filling the spin fluctuations become strong: for n = 0.7-0.9 at T/t = 0.14 they enhance the susceptibility peak up to sevenfold and raise the momentum-dependent part of the scattering rate to four to five times its second-order value. They are driven by an effective spin interaction screened to about 2U/3 and nearly uniform over the zone. Yet the peak height is set by the slightly smaller value of this interaction at the peak wave vector, and near magnetic order this small difference changes the height by a large factor. Two-particle self-consistent theory reproduces the peak because its sum rule fixes its single constant interaction near this value, but for n = 0.7-0.9 at T/t = 0.14 its self-energy overestimates the local scattering rate and underestimates the momentum-dependent part. Though strong, the fluctuations are short ranged, with a correlation length of at most about two lattice spacings, and for n = 0.7-0.9 and T/t >= 0.14 the scattering rate near the Fermi surface varies by at most about 1% at fixed band energy, without hot spots. At U/t = 4 dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) reproduces the local scattering rate and quasiparticle weight within a few percent, and the nonlocal part it misses is approximately a function of the band energy. Strong spin fluctuations thus coexist with nearly isotropic quasiparticles, and the results provide a benchmark for extensions of DMFT and for spin-fluctuation theories.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Emergent Active-Blob Length Scale Governs the Collapse Transition of Tangentially Driven Polymers
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The coil-to-globule transition is a paradigmatic phenomenon in polymer physics and biophysics, in which polymer chains evolve from swollen to globular conformations upon decreasing solvent quality. At equilibrium, this transition can be rationalized in terms of a thermal blob length that diverges at the so-called $\Theta$ condition, marking the crossover from self-avoiding to globular conformations. How activity modifies this conformational transition and affects the fundamental length scales at play remains poorly understood. Here, we address this question for tangentially driven polymers using Brownian dynamics simulations, systematically varying both intrachain attraction strength and activity. We find that polar activity smears out the crossover from swollen to globular conformations. Between self-avoiding and $\Theta$ conditions, activity dominates by introducing an emergent folding length scale, which acts as an active blob length. In this regime, we demonstrate that the ratio of thermal to active length scales provides a new scaling variable that leads to a universal master curve for active polymer collapse.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Suppression and reemergence of directional transport across the ferromagnetic transition in SrRuO$_3$
arXiv_CondMat.summary: SrRuO$_3$ is a canonical itinerant ferromagnet that continues to serve as a fertile platform for exploring spin-orbit coupled transport and topological responses in correlated oxide metals. Here, we investigate a (110)-oriented epitaxial SrRuO3 thin film on DyScO$_3$, where crystallographic anisotropy allows for symmetry-resolved charge transport along orthogonal in-plane directions. We uncover two principal findings. First, the resistance above the Curie temperature $T_{c,on}\approx 165$ K exhibits strong anisotropy, consistent with directionally dependent spin-fluctuation scattering. Below $T_{c,on}$, this anisotropy nearly vanishes, despite persistent structural inequivalence, due to isotropic electron-magnon and electron-electron scattering processes. Second, the application of a magnetic field reveals a striking directional contrast in the linear magnetoresistance (MR): it remains negative and saturates along [001], but changes sign and becomes positive along $[1\bar{1}0]$ below $T_0=145$ K. In contrast, the quadratic MR term is identical for both directions and peaks near $T_{\mathrm{OHE}}^*=155$ K, where the ordinary Hall coefficient crosses zero, consistent with carrier compensation under a two-band scenario. A sign change in the anomalous Hall signal at $T_{\mathrm{AHE}}^*=150$ K is consistent with a temperature-dependent redistribution of Berry-curvature contributions near the Fermi level. These results establish ferromagnetic ordering as the primary driver of the observed directional magnetotransport in SrRuO$_3$.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Accelerating real-time hybrid-functional calculations with learned ACE and symmetry-based FFT reuse
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Real-time hybrid-functional calculations require repeated reconstruction of nonlocal exchange, whose cost grows rapidly with Brillouin-zone sampling. We develop two methods to improve the efficiency of time evolution and spatial processing. The first learns the time evolution of adaptively compressed exchange (ACE) factors and predicts their updates, reducing the frequency of explicit reconstruction. The second uses crystal symmetry to reuse exchange fast Fourier transforms (FFTs) among equivalent real-space points. This symmetry-based FFT reuse (SBFR) reduces the number of FFTs while retaining the full $\bm k$-point sum. The methods can be used with a variety of hybrid functionals, and we use HSE06 in this work. Relative to an ACE reference using full-row mesh FFTs, learned prediction provides more than fivefold acceleration, SBFR more than fourteenfold, and their combination more than sixty-threefold. The combined method shows efficient parallel scaling. After learning, propagation takes less than 0.5 s per step. The reduced computational cost allows us to study nonlinear and nonequilibrium electron dynamics with hybrid functionals and to examine the role of excitonic effects in semiconductors and insulators.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Collective Hall quantization in 3D Chern vector systems
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Understanding the three-dimensional (3D) quantum Hall effect, characterized by a Chern vector rather than a single Chern number, has been a central pursuit in topological physics. While quantized Hall transport is established for the special case with one nonzero Chern component, recent realizations of more general Chern-vector states raise a fundamental question: how does such topology protect quantized transport? Here, we predict a distinct 3D quantized Hall effect protected by $\mathbf{C}=(0,m,n)$. For samples with dimensions $L_y$ and $L_z$, global topology enforces collective quantization of $mL_y+nL_z$, despite the fragility of individual edge modes to disorder. This reveals a novel transport regime in which robust quantization emerges as a holistic property of a unified chiral network,rather than of its constituent modes. Crucially, this collective response manifests as a quantized Hall conductance $G_{xy}=\pm(mL_y+nL_z)e^2/h$, with a distinctive dependence on both Chern-vector components and sample dimensions. We propose candidate materials to facilitate experimental observation.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Atomic identification via the Prandtl-Tomlinson stick-slip mechanism
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Distinguishing atomic species is an ongoing challenge in the field of scanning probe microscopy. Typically, atomic force microscopy makes use of electrostatic interactions to perform atomic identification. Here we perform lateral force microscopy (LFM) measurements with a CO terminated tip of a partially oxidized Cu(110) surface and show clear differences between the metal and oxygen sites over a large z-range. This allows for atomic identification on a typical metal oxide. Density functional theory based calculations show that the tip-sample interaction is dominated by short-ranged orbital interactions and that the electrostatic contribution is negligible. At small tip-sample distances, LFM can probe the Prandtl-Tomlinson stick-slip mechanism on the single-atom scale. It is visible as a striking asymmetry in the forward and backward scan directions, experimentally revealing this fundamental model for nanotribology on the single-atom scale.

arXiv_CondMat.title: A Transport-Information Framework for Continuous-Fiber-Aligned Coarse-Graining Representation Sets
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Consider representation sets of interest whose elements are associated with continuous realizations related to them through coarse-graining (CG). CG can be regarded as an operation that reduces a representation by discarding information that is not retained in its output. However, a systematic description of the information structure associated with CG in general remains to be established. Here, we propose a transport-information framework for continuous-fiber-aligned representation sets, in which each representation is associated with a continuous realization through a fiber structure, with CG defining the projection onto the representation. Within this framework, CG is described through a local-map operation that transports continuous probability mass onto representative points. The resulting transport cost is expressed as the contraction of the second-moment structure of the underlying continuous representation with the transport metric. Building on the previously proposed framework of unavoidable canonical nonlinearity (UCN), this construction provides a non-arbitrary information-theoretic interpretation of the CG-associated transport cost in terms of information indistinguishability, quantified by an expected Kullback-Leibler divergence associated with the CG geometry. The present framework provides a basis for describing information costs associated with individual CG operations and for comparing representation sets while accounting for their underlying continuous realizations.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Emergent non-reciprocal pair interactions in catalytically propelled active polyhedra
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Particle shape plays a fundamental role in the dynamics and pair interactions of active particles. Yet, experimental measurements of anisotropic active particles are largely lacking. Here, we introduce an experimental system that allows us to observe and measure the effective pair interactions of self-propelled active colloidal polyhedra. We realize such a system by 3D micro-printing quasi- 2D polyhedral colloids with edge number N= 3,4,5,6 and infinity and induce propulsion by partially coating them with an iridium catalytic cap and dispersing them in hydrazine. Despite their different geometries, all shapes exhibit similar single-particle positional dynamics. Stochastic Force Inference reveals predominantly radial, non-reciprocal pair interactions with similar attractive and repulsive regimes for all particle shapes at center-to center distances of about two particle diameters. A minimal plausible phoretic active-Brownian-particle model with a disc shape reproduces the experimentally observed behavior and identifies the physical origins: concentration-dependent slowing down sets their dominant angular symmetry, while the spatial geometry of the chemical coupling and phoretic attraction recover their relative magnitudes and angular dependence. We find that the shape anisotropy present in experiments only modulates the magnitudes and angular dependence of these interactions, and that these variations become more pronounced the stronger the anisotropy. Our results demonstrate the interplay of chemically mediated interactions and particle geometry-induced effects at intermediate interaction distances.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Luther-Emery liquid in one-dimensional attractive Fermi gas
arXiv_CondMat.summary: One-dimensional (1D) interacting Fermi gases underpin a rich variety of quantum liquids, ranging from the Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid and the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov paired state to the Luther-Emery liquid (LEL). Notably, the LEL-characterized by gapless excitations in charge or spin degree of freedom and gapped excitations in the other-has long been theoretically predicted but has eluded definitive experimental observation to date. By exactly solving the attractive Yang-Gaudin model via the Bethe ansatz, we fully determine the low-energy excitation spectra for both spin and charge channels. For fully paired fermions, the spectrum features gapped spin excitation coexisting with gapless charge excitation. We further employ bosonization to derive analytical expressions for the dynamical structure factor (DSF) of the gapped spin excitation, which is a long-standing challenge in this study. In the trapped gas, we find that the spin Bragg spectroscopy peak occurs at a much higher frequency than the charge-mode peak, where the splitting frequency between these two peaks scales approximately linearly with the interaction strength. Crucially, the spin gap manifests as a sharp threshold in the spin DSF, below which spectral weight is completely absent, proving a direct and unambiguous spectroscopic fingerprint of the LEL. Our work establishes quasi-1D trapped attractive Fermi gases as a pristine experimental platform for the long-sought direct observation of the LEL.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Quantum Fluctuations and Wigner Dynamics of a Carbon Nanotube Oscillator Driven by an Atomic Force Microscope
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Suspended carbon nanotubes provide a useful platform for studying controlled nanomechanical motion in regimes where environmental fluctuations, memory effects, and quantum coherence can all influence the dynamics. We model the fundamental flexural mode of a carbon nanotube driven by an atomic force microscope as a harmonic quantum Brownian oscillator subject to a prescribed classical force and coupled linearly to a thermal environment. Starting from the generalized Langevin equation, we formulate the reduced dynamics directly in phase space, where the Wigner function evolves through a Gaussian propagator determined by dissipative linear transport, a deterministic force-induced displacement, and bath-induced fluctuations. For a Drude memory kernel, the retarded response is expressed through the three roots of a characteristic cubic equation. In the classical-noise limit, the three independent entries of the finite-time covariance matrix reduce to explicit finite sums over these response poles, eliminating numerical double-time covariance integration. We extend the construction to the full quantum fluctuation spectrum, obtaining a thermal frequency series representation that retains zero-point and low-temperature fluctuations. For an initial two-packet superposition, we examine interference attenuation and the integrated negative part of the Wigner function, which provides a phase space measure of nonclassicality. These results provide an explicit analytical framework for finite-memory quantum Brownian motion of bound oscillators and a tractable phase space description of driven carbon nanotube dynamics relevant to future quantum state preparation and quantum tomography experiments.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Large Deviations in Stochastic Dynamics: A Hamiltonian Perspective
arXiv_CondMat.summary: These lecture notes present an introduction to large deviations in stochastic dynamical systems, adapted from a lecture series given at the Les Houches school ``Large Deviations: Theory and Applications'' in July 2024. The exposition develops the theory through a unified methodology: WKB analysis of backward Kolmogorov equations, which reveals the Hamiltonian structure underlying all large deviation principles considered here. We treat three asymptotic regimes systematically. First, the small-noise limit for stochastic differential equations and the large-volume limit for Markov jump processes, where the Large Deviation Principle emerges from the Law of Large Numbers through progressively finer characterizations of fluctuations. Second, the long-time limit combined with small noise, yielding the quasipotential formalism for metastability and transition rates in both equilibrium and nonequlibrium systems. Third, the long-time limit at finite noise, connecting to spectral methods via tilted generators and enabling reduction of multiscale systems.We survey computational approaches including minimum action methods, their geometric variants for quasipotential calculations, and neural network techniques. The Schl\"{o}gl model of chemical bistability serves as a running example, illustrating both scalar and spatially extended settings. Appendices provide self-contained background on stochastic calculus and Markov jump processes.

arXiv_CondMat.title: The optical force on a dielectric slab
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Radiation-pressure forces on transmissive optics, including dynamical backaction, are usually computed from the momentum flux of the external fields. For a dielectric of finite thickness, this omits the time dependence of the electromagnetic momentum stored inside. We compute the force on a lossless dielectric slab of arbitrary thickness $L_s$ submerged in a dielectric fluid, proceeding from both Lorentz force on its bound charges and from the external momentum fluxes for arbitrary carrier and sideband fields. We treat the surrounding medium through a prescribed linear dielectric response and do not model the accompanying mechanical response of the fluid, including pressure and electrostriction. These two methods both recover the expected force in the limit of a thin reflector, but differ in the more general case by the rate of change of the field momentum stored in the slab. This storage term vanishes for static fields and at low frequencies reduces to $(L_s/c^2)\,dP/dt$, where $P$ is the net power through the slab. In a cavity, where $P$ depends on the slab position, the storage term produces a velocity-dependent force. The Abraham and Minkowski momentum formulations applied to the storage term are reconciled to give an unambiguous force on the dielectric in the case of an exterior vacuum environment, where there is no fluid response to model.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Physics-Inspired Optimizers beyond the Edge of Stability: Period-Two Orbits and Delayed Instability
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Gradient descent with momentum can be viewed as a particle moving with friction in the loss landscape. In deep learning the learning rate is usually large, so training is a discrete dynamical system: in many full-batch experiments the sharpness grows to the optimizer's stability limit, the edge of stability (EoS), and training continues there. Physics-inspired optimizers change this motion; Velocity-Regularized Adam (VRAdam), for example, shrinks the step at high speed. We study kinetic maps, in which the step is the gradient of a kinetic energy of the momentum, and ask what they do beyond the EoS. (i) In a reduced model, a kinetic map creates a symmetric period-two orbit beyond the edge, strictly linearly stable if and only if the map's elasticity (the log-log slope of step length versus momentum) lies between 0 and 1; on it, training sits at an effective edge of stability. VRAdam's damper fails above twice the critical learning rate, where its kinetic energy is not convex; the Legendre dual of VRAdam's own Lagrangian is convex and passes at every learning rate. (ii) Because the sharpness rises gradually, the loss of stability is delayed, as in Neishtadt's theory of slowly swept bifurcations. In a network with a controlled sweep, the dynamics match this theory without fitted parameters, including the memory of where the sweep started and its erasure by noise. (iii) With momentum, reaching the oscillation also requires elasticity at large momentum: maps that bound the step have competing period-four and chaotic attractors already at beta1 = 0.9, while the cubic-Legendre map reached the oscillation from every sampled start up to beta1 = 0.99. Experiments on an exact quadratic problem, a full-batch MLP and ResNet-32 support the theory; on ResNet-18, much of the apparent benefit of the maps is reproduced by matching the effective learning rate.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Nonlocality effects on fermions confined within a hard-wall potential
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We investigate nonlocality effects on the energy spectrum of spin-$1/2$ fermions confined by hard-wall potentials. Starting from a nonlocal Dirac theory with a modified kinetic term, we formulate the associated field equation in flat spacetime using cylindrical coordinates. By exploiting the eigenvalue spectrum of the squared Dirac operator, the original infinite-order equation is reduced to a finite-order problem. We also show that on the branch continuously connected to the local Dirac theory the nonlocal corrections can be encoded in an effective fermion mass. We then find analytical energy spectra for two confining geometries: a cylindrical hard wall and a quantum ring defined by two concentric cylindrical boundaries. In both cases, the radial equations reduce to Bessel equations and the boundary conditions quantize the allowed modes. The local hard-wall spectra are recovered for $\Lambda\to\infty$, whereas finite nonlocality shifts the mass contribution and, consequently, the particle--antiparticle energy separation. These results provide a direct characterization of nonlocal effects in quantum-confined fermionic systems.
authors: G. Q. Garcia, P. J. Porf\'irio

arXiv_CondMat.title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
arXiv_CondMat.summary: The physics of interacting baths is of interest in a variety of contexts, ranging from ultracold atoms to ionized gases. While many features can already be captured in a one-dimensional model, others are specific to the situation of two or three-dimensional systems. In this paper, we focus on three-dimensional features of a model for thermalization between two baths that we have explored in earlier publications. In contrast to the one-dimensional situation we show that, en route to thermalization, deviations from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions more akin to $\kappa$-distributions are observed. In three dimensions, these can be seen in changes at the peak of the distribution, which is precluded by the expected monotonic behavior of the energy distributions in one dimension. Furthermore, we consider thermalization for anisotropic trapping and explore its role in the onset of anomalous scaling with respect to the particle number. These results may be pertinent to the understanding of the interplay between turbulent behavior and nonlinearities for a variety of many-body classical systems.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Generation of non-Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions during thermalization of interacting baths
arXiv_CondMat.summary: We report on numerical experiments of thermalization between two reservoirs in which interspecies interactions are mediated via a Hamiltonian with a Gaussian dependence upon the distance between the particles. By using relatively high statistics, we are able to study deviations from the initially imprinted Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions as a function of the range and strength of the interaction, as well as the parameters of the two baths such as masses, trapping frequencies, that strongly affect the spatial overlap of the two species. At large interaction strengths and for any range, deviations are attributable to the sudden conversion of latent interaction energy into kinetic energy of the particles. In addition, long range interactions generate deviations even for interaction strengths in the weak regime, and non-uniform confinement introduces a further source of deviation from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution. This latter results in transient two temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions suggestive of an inverse cascading route from inter-particle dynamics to thermalization. In the weakly-interacting regime, a simple expression for the equilibrium temperature is also obtained and discussed. These findings may be of relevance in the dynamics of exothermic chemical reactions, in the physics of ultracold atomic mixtures, and in self-sustained burning plasmas.

arXiv_CondMat.title: Systematic Truncated Wigner Approximation for Open Spin Systems Reveals Long-Range Order Far from Equilibrium
arXiv_CondMat.summary: Long-range interactions can protect dissipative order against fluctuations, but determining when they do so in two dimensions remains out of reach for existing many-body methods. We develop a continuous SU(2)-covariant truncated-Wigner framework that maps the problem onto stochastic dynamics with one Bloch sphere per site. Derived systematically from the exact Stratonovich-Weyl evolution of the Lindblad equation, it generates both drift and reservoir noise for arbitrary spin $S$. Benchmarks against exact and tensor-network calculations validate its description of non-equilibrium dynamics and steady states. Applied to 400-site two-dimensional dissipative anisotropic XY lattices, our method reveals physics missed by mean-field and perturbative approaches: vortex-antivortex proliferation destroys the predicted staggered-XY phase for nearest-neighbour coupling, whereas algebraically decaying interactions stabilize an extended $\mathbb{Z}_2$-ordered phase. We obtain the first beyond-mean-field steady-state phase diagram of the long-range interacting model, revealing reentrant loss of order at strong coupling and closure of the ordered region beyond $\alpha\approx 3.5$.
